sections.title: Walk the flowchart
sections.intro: kubectl works, but it feels sluggish. Sometimes a `kubectl apply` hangs for several seconds, and once a write failed outright. Someone says "probably etcd." Don't take that on faith.

questions.prompt: "Feels slow" is your only evidence so far. What's the first move?
options: Get a direct etcd reading and rule out your own network
Restore from the latest snapshot to be safe
Restart apiserver to reset its etcd connections
Defrag etcd — it's the most common fix
questions.explanation: "Slow" is a real early etcd signal, but it's vague. Your own VPN makes kubectl feel just as slow. Every fix in this file has a cost, so confirm first.

questions.prompt: You SSH to a control-plane node and run `etcdctl endpoint health`. It fails. Before concluding etcd is down, what might be wrong with the check itself?
questions.snippet:
{"level":"warn","msg":"retrying of unary invoker failed","error":"context deadline exceeded"}
Error: unhealthy cluster
options: The location — etcdctl must run inside a pod
The API version — set `ETCDCTL_API=2`
Nothing — etcd is down
The check — on kubeadm, etcdctl needs the TLS cert flags
questions.explanation: A misconfigured health check can look exactly like an outage. Always rule out your instrument before you trust what it reports.

questions.prompt: With certs, it responds, but slowly, with warnings. Which half of the fork are you in, and how urgent is it?
questions.snippet: https://10.0.1.11:2379 is healthy: successfully committed proposal: took = 1.8s
options: Healthy — 1.8s is a normal commit time
Off-path — the slowness is apiserver's
Degraded but responding — a resource problem
Unresponsive — quorum is lost, page everyone
questions.explanation: It committed a proposal, so there's a leader and a working majority. A healthy commit takes milliseconds, and 1.8s points at a resource problem: usually disk, sometimes database size.

questions.prompt: The etcd logs show this repeatedly. What resource is the bottleneck, and why does etcd care so much about it?
questions.snippet:
{"level":"warn","msg":"apply request took too long","took":"1.2s","expected-duration":"100ms"}
{"level":"warn","msg":"failed to send out heartbeat on time (exceeded the 100ms timeout for 800.1ms)"}
options: Network bandwidth between the members
CPU — etcd's consensus is compute-heavy
Memory — the keyspace no longer fits in RAM
Disk write latency — every write is fsync'd
questions.explanation: etcd's durability guarantee is a synchronous disk write. Network-attached or shared spinning disks are the classic cause. The fix is faster dedicated storage, and you take a snapshot before migrating the data directory.

questions.prompt: Next week, a different symptom: writes fail outright, reads still work. You check alarms. What does this mean, and is your disk full?
questions.snippet:
$ etcdctl alarm list
memberID:8e9e05c52164694d alarm:NOSPACE

$ df -h /var/lib/etcd
/dev/sda1  100G  14G  86G  14% /
options: Quorum loss — a member stopped accepting writes
Not the disk — the DB hit its storage quota
The disk is full — free space and it recovers
A false positive — disarm it and move on
questions.explanation: 86G free proves this isn't the disk. NOSPACE is about `--quota-backend-bytes`. Disarming without shrinking the DB just re-trips the alarm on the next write.

questions.prompt: apiserver already compacts etcd every 5 minutes. So why is the database still at the quota?
questions.snippet:
$ etcdctl endpoint status --write-out=table
| ENDPOINT            | DB SIZE | DB SIZE IN USE |
| https://10.0.1.11   | 2.1 GB  | 310 MB         |
options: Compaction is broken and needs restarting
The quota is miscalculated on this version
The cluster really holds 2.1 GB of live objects
Compaction frees space inside the file; only defrag shrinks it
questions.explanation: Total size vs. in-use size is the tell (if your table doesn't show the in-use column, `-w json` has `dbSizeInUse`). Defrag reclaims that space, then `etcdctl alarm disarm` re-enables writes. Raise the quota only if the in-use size genuinely needs it.

questions.prompt: You're about to defrag. How do you run it on a 3-member cluster?
options: Only on the leader, since it owns the data
Only on followers — never touch the leader
One member at a time, waiting for each to recover
All three at once, to finish quickly
questions.explanation: A blocked member is temporarily a failed member. With three, you can afford one at a time and no more.

questions.prompt: Worst case, months later: two of three members are gone after a storage failure. apiserver returns `etcdserver: request timed out`, and no member reports itself as leader. What's the order of operations?
options: Add two new empty members to regain quorum
Recover members first; restore from snapshot last
Restart apiserver until it reconnects
Restore from the latest snapshot immediately
questions.explanation: A restore always loses the writes made since the last snapshot, so it's the last resort. Adding empty members doesn't work, because joining a cluster needs an existing quorum to approve the change. This is also why how often you take snapshots is a real operational decision.

sections.title: Read the signal
sections.intro: Each one stands alone. Degraded, quorum, or not etcd at all?

questions.prompt: Is the cluster serving requests right now?
questions.snippet:
$ etcdctl member list
1, started, etcd-1, ...
2, started, etcd-2, ...
3, unstarted, etcd-3, ... unreachable
options: Partly — only reads work without all members
Yes — 2 of 3 is a majority, but there's no slack left
No — any member down blocks all writes
Partly — only writes work, reads go stale
questions.explanation: Quorum is a majority, not all members. One more failure right now would mean real quorum loss, which is why this is urgent even though nothing looks broken.

questions.prompt: Your team wants to grow from 3 etcd members to 4 "for more resilience." Good idea?
options: Yes — four members means one more spare
It makes no difference either way
Yes — even numbers elect leaders faster
No — 4 needs 3 for quorum, so it still tolerates only 1
questions.explanation: 2f + 1 members tolerate f failures: 3 tolerates 1, 5 tolerates 2, and 4 is no better than 3.

questions.prompt: Every member says it's healthy on its own, but there's no leader. The logs show this. What's broken?
questions.snippet: {"level":"warn","msg":"failed to dial","peer-id":"a3f...","error":"x509: certificate signed by unknown authority"}
options: Client TLS — apiserver's etcd certs are bad
The quota — writes are blocked cluster-wide
Disk latency — elections keep timing out
Peer TLS — members can't talk to each other
questions.explanation: Peer traffic (port 2380) and client traffic (2379) use separate certs and separate network paths. Checking only the client side is how this gets misdiagnosed.

questions.prompt: kubectl doesn't respond at all: "connection refused." Should you start with etcd?
options: apiserver first — refused means it isn't running
Restore a snapshot first, then investigate
etcd first — it's the source of truth
The scheduler first — it owns placement
questions.explanation: Work from what you can observe. You can only get to etcd through apiserver's evidence, or by going straight to the node. Jumping ahead skips the cheap checks.

questions.prompt: New pods aren't being scheduled, but kubectl is fast and writes succeed. Is this an etcd problem?
options: Yes — it's the NOSPACE quota again
No — fast, successful writes mean etcd is fine
Yes — etcd is silently dropping new pods
Yes — a member is down and lagging
questions.explanation: Fast, successful writes are strong evidence that etcd is healthy. The symptom families are different: missing actions point to 03, slow or failing storage points to 04.

questions.prompt: The logs show frequent `elected leader` / `lost leader` messages, but every member is up. What's the usual root cause?
options: Too many members competing to lead
An expired CA on one of the members
The NOSPACE alarm forcing re-elections
Slow disk fsync making heartbeats miss their deadline
questions.explanation: Leader churn often looks like a membership problem but is usually a resource problem underneath. Check the disk latency warnings before touching membership.
